OurBigBook.com Words: 752k Articles: 14k
Physics investigates matter, motion, and interactions by building mathematical models and testing their consequences against observations. A physical law supplies a relation; a model specifies the objects, conditions, and approximations used to apply it. Classical mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics organize different aspects of these investigations. Their usefulness comes from turning measurements into predictions that can be checked and refined.
Consider a simple pendulum: how does its oscillation period change when its length changes? For small amplitude, the ideal model gives T0​=2πℓ/g​, where g is gravitational acceleration. Taking g=9.81m/s2 as the model parameter, a one-metre pendulum has predicted period 2.0061s. Increasing its length to four metres gives 4.0121s: quadrupling the length doubles the period. The point mass cancels from the equation, so changing it alone does not change this model's answer.
The prediction identifies a mechanism and a way to challenge it. The small-angle approximation replaces sinθ by θ; the full ideal equation predicts a longer period at large amplitude. At 60∘, its period is about 1.07318T0​, already a 7.3% change. Measurements at such amplitudes can reveal the limit of the approximation, while appreciable drag requires a damped pendulum. These distinctions are developed in simple pendulum and dimensional analysis. The small-amplitude model is also derived in Ling, Sanny and Moebs, University Physics, pendulums.
Several different experiments can become one calculation. Nondimensionalization rewrites the pendulum equation using τ=tg/ℓ​, leaving d2θ/dτ2+sinθ=0. All lengths share that dimensionless equation; the amplitude remains a parameter. Similarly, conservation laws and symmetry reveal features that many models share. This is one source of the subject's beauty: a compact relation can organize a large range of phenomena.
The connection to evidence remains essential when a model is elegant. In his introductory lectures, Richard Feynman emphasizes testing proposed relations by experiment and using idealizations whose accuracy depends on the conditions. [ref] A discrepancy can motivate a better measurement, a better approximation, or a different physical model; the mathematical calculation and the empirical assessment are both part of the explanation.

Its predictions must be compared with physical observations.

In general relativity, the metric tensor describes gravitational effects, and tidal forces are encoded by spacetime curvature.

Physics OurBigBook.com
A plasma is a gas of mobile charged particles whose collective electromagnetic response is important to its dynamics. It commonly contains ions and Electrons, and may also contain a neutral component: complete ionization is not required. A multi-species fluid description has current density J=∑s​qs​ns​us​. The relative motion of the species can matter even when a single-fluid magnetohydrodynamics approximation describes the large-scale dynamics.

Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The plasma frequency is the characteristic electrostatic oscillation frequency of a charged species displaced against a neutralizing background. For number density ns​, charge qs​ and mass ms​, the displayed formula uses SI units; in Gaussian units it is ωps​=4πns​qs2​/ms​​. The ion skin depth is c/ωpi​ for the ion species. Different species have different plasma frequencies.

Ion skin depth (di​=c/ωpi​)

Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
For a singly charged ion species in Gaussian units, ωpi​=(4πne2/mi​)1/2 is its plasma frequency and di​=cmi​/(4πne2)​. The ion skin depth marks a characteristic scale below which ion and electron motion can separate in a magnetized plasma. Together with the Alfvén speed, it satisfies vA​di​=cB0​/(4πen), the coefficient of guide-field propagation in electron magnetohydrodynamics.

The joule is the SI unit of energy, work, and heat. One newton of force acting along one metre of displacement does one joule of work. The relation 1J=1Nm makes mechanical and electrical transfers comparable in the same energy unit. [ref]

Philosophy of physics

Words: 285 Articles: 4
Physics OurBigBook.com
Philosophy of physics studies the interpretation and explanatory structure of physical theories, including the relation between mathematical models, observable phenomena and claims about what exists. Its questions include theoretical reduction, emergence and competing formulations of physical locality.

Stochastic Einstein locality

Words: 65
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A formulation of stochastic Einstein locality restricts an event's objective chance to its relevant causal past, rather than spacelike-separated interventions or facts. Different versions constrain either marginal chances or joint conditional probabilities. A one-wing marginal condition alone does not supply outcome independence. To derive a Bell theorem by this route, the proposed locality assumptions must include the appropriate screening-off relation for the two outcomes, together with a common setting-independent past distribution.

Reichenbach common cause principle

Words: 76
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A classical common-cause explanation seeks past variables which screen off a correlation: conditioned on a sufficiently complete common cause, the correlated events become independent. A Bell local causality model adds local dependence on settings and a single compatible past-variable distribution for all measurement contexts. Providing a different setting-dependent screening variable for each pair of settings does not establish that stronger Bell model. The distinction between a causal mechanism and a purely probabilistic screening construction matters when interpreting this principle.

Emergence

Words: 57
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Emergence concerns novel collective patterns or explanatory structures relative to a lower-level description. Robust effective behaviour can emerge through coarse-graining or singular limits while remaining derivable from the microscopic theory. The stronger claim that genuinely new causal powers cannot be reduced to that theory requires an additional argument; nonanalyticity of a limiting function alone does not establish it.

Theoretical reduction

Words: 55
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Theoretical reduction relates theories by deriving the laws or predictions of one from another together with explicit identifications of quantities and appropriate domain assumptions. A reduction can require approximation, coarse-graining or a limiting construction. Deduction of an ideal limiting model is different from exact deduction of the same properties for every finite member of a model sequence.

Nuclear physics

Physics OurBigBook.com
The study of atomic nuclei, their structure, reactions and interactions. Nuclear forces between nucleons and nuclear binding energies connect it to the low-energy consequences of Quantum chromodynamics.

Mössbauer effect

Words: 55
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nucleus bound in a solid can emit or absorb a photon without exciting lattice vibrations, transferring momentum to the solid as a whole. The resulting recoil energy is negligible compared with the isolated-nucleus recoil, making very narrow resonant emission and absorption lines observable. The Pound-Rebka experiment uses this effect to resolve the small frequency shift from gravitational redshift.

Nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE)

Words: 247 Articles: 3
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
At sufficiently high temperature and density, forward and inverse nuclear reactions can balance so that abundances are determined by thermodynamic conditions, nuclear binding and conserved quantities. Silicon burning approaches such an equilibrium among iron-group nuclei. Weak reactions can separately change the electron fraction, so the favored mixture need not be pure iron.

Words: 91
Nuclear statistical equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Nickel-56 and iron-54 have the same neutron number and differ by two protons. Dividing their nuclear statistical equilibrium abundance formulas cancels the neutron density and leaves the displayed ratio, with ΔB=B56​−B54​ and K containing temperature-independent statistical and mass factors in the simplified model. For material with equal total proton and neutron numbers and only these nuclei plus free protons, charge balance gives np​=2n54​. Thus n56​/n543​∝T−3eΔB/(kT). This has a finite temperature maximum only if the signed energy difference is negative; conventional positive total nuclear binding energies for these two actual isotopes instead give a positive difference.

Nuclear statistical equilibrium OurBigBook.com
For electrically neutral fully ionized matter, Ye​ is the number of electrons, or total protons, per baryon. With isotope mass fractions Xi​, charge numbers Zi​ and mass numbers Ai​, the displayed sum neglects small nuclear mass-defect corrections. Strong and electromagnetic reactions preserve it, while electron capture and beta-plus decay reduce it. The proton-to-neutron number ratio is Ye​/(1−Ye​).

Words: 52
Electron fraction in stellar matter OurBigBook.com
The neutron excess is the number of neutrons minus protons per baryon. A mixture of carbon-12 and oxygen-16 has zero neutron excess, while neon-22 contributes 2/22 per baryon in that isotope. Thus a neon-22 mass fraction X22​ gives η=X22​/11. A nonzero excess shifts iron-group ashes from symmetric nickel-56 toward neutron-rich isotopes, even before additional weak reactions occur.

Words: 38
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Capture of a neutron increases mass number without immediately changing atomic number. It avoids the charged-particle Coulomb barrier. Subsequent beta-minus decay can increase atomic number. Whether capture is slow or fast compared with relevant beta decays distinguishes the slow neutron-capture process from the rapid neutron-capture process.

Nucleosynthesis

Words: 233 Articles: 4
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Nucleosynthesis is the production of atomic nuclei through nuclear reactions. It includes Big Bang nucleosynthesis, stellar nucleosynthesis and production in explosive or compact-remnant environments. Making nuclei and delivering them to the interstellar medium are separate steps in chemical enrichment.

Stellar nucleosynthesis

Words: 204 Articles: 3
Nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Stellar nucleosynthesis encompasses nuclear production during stellar evolution and explosions, including hydrogen burning, core helium burning, advanced burning and neutron-capture processes. Stellar mass, composition, mixing and mass loss govern which nuclei form and which eventually escape. Slow neutron-capture process and rapid neutron-capture process build many nuclei beyond the iron group.
Neon-22 neutron excess from nitrogen-14 (X22​=1422​X14​,Ye​=21​−14X14​​)
Words: 68
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Two alpha captures and an intervening beta-plus decay turn each nitrogen-14 nucleus into neon-22, incorporating eight baryons from helium and converting one proton to a neutron. With no loss or dilution and nuclear mass defects neglected, a nitrogen-14 mass fraction X14​ therefore yields neon-22 mass fraction (22/14)X14​, not X14​. In otherwise symmetric carbon-oxygen matter this gives the displayed electron fraction in stellar matter. A final neon mass fraction and a pre-helium-burning metallicity must not silently be treated as identical.
Gamma-process nucleosynthesis
Words: 44
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Hot explosive material can use photodisintegration on pre-existing heavy seed nuclei through neutron, proton and alpha emission. This gamma process supplies some proton-rich isotopes that the principal neutron-capture paths bypass. It is a particular mechanism, rather than a synonym for every proposed proton-rich nucleosynthetic process.
r-process (r-process)
Words: 53
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
At sufficiently large neutron density, successive neutron captures outrun relevant beta decays and produce very neutron-rich nuclei. Decay toward stability afterward yields many heavy isotopes, including some actinides. Neutron-rich ejecta from neutron star mergers provide an established site; particular magnetically driven collapse outflows are additional candidates. This does not imply that every ordinary core-collapse supernova produces a complete heavy-element pattern.

Nuclear reaction

Words: 41
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nuclear reaction transforms one or more atomic nuclei through interactions with particles or other nuclei. Total energy, momentum, electric charge and nucleon number constrain ordinary low-energy reaction bookkeeping. Nuclear fusion, alpha capture, neutron capture and photodisintegration are important examples in stellar nucleosynthesis. Weak processes can also change the proton-to-neutron ratio.

Beta-minus decay (n⟶p+e−+νe​)

Words: 35
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
An energetically allowed weak transition converts a neutron into a proton, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. Free neutron decay is an example; in nuclei, the nuclear binding energy determines whether the transition is possible.

Nuclear fusion (Q=(minitial​−mfinal​)c2)

Words: 131 Articles: 3
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Fusion combines nuclear reactants into heavier compound nuclei or products. A net decrease in rest mass releases energy; heavier fusion reactions can instead require energy. Stellar nuclear fusion uses exothermic networks to power stars, and quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier permits many charged-particle reactions at stellar temperatures.

Alpha capture (ZA​X+α⟶Z+2A+4​Y+γ)

Nuclear fusion OurBigBook.com
Capture of an alpha particle increases the mass number by four and atomic number by two. Radiative alpha capture releases a photon, while reactions such as (α,n) can instead emit a neutron. Carbon-12 alpha capture competes with helium production of carbon during core helium burning.
Carbon-12 alpha capture (12C(α,γ)16O)
Words: 20
Alpha capture OurBigBook.com
Capture of an alpha particle by carbon-12 makes oxygen-16. Competition between this reaction and the Triple-alpha process helps determine the carbon-to-oxygen ratio after core helium burning.

Nuclear fusion OurBigBook.com
Repulsion between positively charged nuclei creates this electrostatic energy barrier outside the short-range nuclear interaction. Quantum tunnelling allows reaction at thermal energies below its classical height and contributes the penetration factor in the Gamow peak.

Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A sufficiently energetic photon can break up a nucleus, consuming energy for an endothermic breakup. In neon burning and silicon burning, such steps combine with captures to form a larger reaction network whose net energy balance can be positive.

Words: 47
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
An energetically allowed weak nuclear transition converts a proton into a neutron, emitting a positron and electron neutrino. Positron annihilation deposits additional electromagnetic energy, while the neutrino can escape. These transitions are steps of the CNO cycle and the pp III branch; an isolated free proton cannot undergo this decay.

Electron capture (ZA​X+e−⟶Z−1A​Y+νe​)

Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nucleus can capture an electron when energetically allowed, converting a proton into a neutron and emitting an electron neutrino. Beryllium-7 electron capture participates in one of the proton-proton chain branches. Stellar capture rates depend on ionization, mass density and electron phase space.

Nuclear force

Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
The residual strong interaction between nucleons. Its long-distance part involves pion exchange and depends on spin and isospin. It is distinct from directly exchanging gluons between color-singlet nucleons.

Atomic nucleus (A=Z+N)

Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
The central system of protons and neutrons in an atom. Its mass number A is its baryon number in ordinary nuclear states; Z is the proton number and N the neutron number.

Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The helium-four atomic nucleus, containing two protons and two neutrons. Its ground-state spin and isospin are zero. A quantized cubic four-Skyrmion supplies a corresponding nuclear state in the soliton description.

Words: 23
Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The bound atomic nucleus containing one proton and one neutron. Its ground-state spin is one and its isospin is zero. The appropriately quantized toroidal two-Skyrmion models these quantum numbers.

Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The positive energy needed to separate a bound atomic nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons. It is the mass defect times c2. In a Skyrmion model of a nucleus, both separated nucleon masses and the multi-soliton state require a consistent quantization and calibration.

Semiconductor

Words: 140 Articles: 3
Physics OurBigBook.com
A semiconductor has an electronic band gap and a conductivity strongly affected by temperature, impurities and carrier injection. Optical absorption can create mobile electrons and holes, enabling a photodiode.

Acceptor impurity

Words: 42
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can accept an electron from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole. A shallow acceptor creates an impurity level in a crystal near and above the valence-band edge. Donor and acceptor levels are descriptions of appropriate dopants, not universal features of every impurity species.

Donor impurity

Words: 43
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can supply an electron to the conduction band. A shallow donor has a localized occupied impurity level in a crystal near and below the conduction-band edge; thermal or other ionization releases its electron. The binding energy depends on the host dielectric response and effective mass.

Mercury cadmium telluride

Words: 28
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Mercury cadmium telluride is a semiconductor whose composition tunes its band gap and hence its long-wavelength absorption cutoff. It is widely used as the absorbing material in infrared detector arrays.

Acoustics OurBigBook.com
For a slowly varying parallel shear flow U(y)ex​, the leading WKB method neglects mean-velocity gradients while retaining local advection. The continuity equation and linearized Euler equations then give the displayed acoustic dispersion relation. On the positive intrinsic-frequency branch, ω=Ukx​+c0​∣k∣ and the group velocity is Uex​+c0​k/∣k∣. A wavefront normal is parallel to k; the acoustic energy-ray direction generally differs because of the advection term.

Words: 89
Acoustic eikonal equation in a shear flow OurBigBook.com
In a stationary, horizontally homogeneous wall boundary layer, Hamiltonian ray-tracing equations conserve ω and kx​. If U increases away from the wall, downstream-oriented kx​>0 waves have decreasing positive intrinsic frequency and decreasing ky2​. At U=ω/kx​−c0​, the transverse wavenumber vanishes and the acoustic ray turns. For U(0)=0, a downstream launch angle β0​ above the wall can reach a uniform stream of Mach number M∞​ only if cosβ0​≤(1+M∞​)−1. This uses the positive acoustic branch, constant sound speed and no intervening critical layer; a turning point itself requires a uniform local approximation rather than the ordinary WKB method.

Expanding the Neumann boundary condition at z=0 gives ∂z​ψ1​=2Aeiαx(β2h+iαh′). For height transform h(q)=∫h(x)e−iqxdx, the outgoing correction is (2A/(2πi))∫(k2−αq)h(q−α)eiqx+iβ(q)z/β(q)dq, with β(q)=k2−q2​ on the outgoing sheet. Controlled height expansions also require adequate slope and spectral regularity; small incident phase displacement alone does not bound every normal-derivative correction.

Averaging this expression using the power spectrum of surface height gives the displayed coherent reflection coefficient. Thus the root mean square height alone does not fix the coherent mean: the height correlation spectrum matters. For roughness varying slowly enough that q≃α in the integral, rN​≃1−2β2σ2. A local random-height phase average needs this additional approximation and is not a general consequence of stationarity.

Acoustics OurBigBook.com
Sonar uses sound propagation and reflected signals to detect objects or measure distances. Upward-looking sonar can record sea-ice draft along a moving platform's track; beam width, return selection and processing affect the inferred profile.

An acoustic waveguide confines sound transversely while allowing longitudinal propagation. Rigid walls impose a homogeneous normal-velocity condition, producing Neumann transverse modes. Each transverse eigenvalue gives a longitudinal wave number: modes below their cutoff decay evanescently, while cut-on modes carry outgoing sound. An open semi-infinite guide can be studied with the Wiener-Hopf method.

Reflecting the upper-edge coordinates reverses the edge-wave sign. Their path phases are e±ik0​hsinθ. Thus Sommerfeld half-plane diffraction gives the displayed sum, where D(r)=2/(πk0​r)​e−ik0​r−iπ/4. For n>0, the apparent poles at θ=±α are removable in the combined expression, with limit ikhD(r)/2. Single-edge nonuniform far-field poles are not physical infinities. This combined far-field limit assumes a radiation distance beyond the aperture's near field and neglects further edge interactions; it is not uniform at duct cutoff.

An acoustic analogy rearranges fluid conservation equations into a chosen linear acoustic propagation operator plus effective forcing. The rearrangement can be exact before source approximations are made. A term classified as forcing can also contain propagation effects omitted from the reference operator; this produces propagation-source ambiguity in an acoustic analogy. The Lighthill acoustic analogy is a familiar homogeneous reference-medium example.

For example, a homogeneous-Laplacian operator with spatially varying reference sound speed omits the first-gradient terms of the stratified acoustic pressure equation. These terms then reappear as effective forcing, even for a freely propagating small disturbance in a static medium. A right-hand-side term is therefore not automatically an independent physical noise source.

It catches impossible equations and reveals scaling before a full dynamical calculation. Adding two quantities requires the same physical dimension; replacing metres by centimetres must change numerical values consistently while preserving physical predictions.
For the ideal simple pendulum, suppose its oscillation period T depends only on mass m, length ℓ, gravitational acceleration g, and dimensionless angular amplitude θ0​. Write T=maℓbgcF(θ0​). Since [m]=M, [ℓ]=L, and [g]=LT−2, matching physical dimensions gives a=0, b+c=0, and −2c=1. Consequently
T=gℓ​​F(θ0​).
(10)
The angular amplitude is dimensionless when expressed in radians. Dimensional analysis establishes the length/gravity scaling and the absence of a mass factor under these assumptions, but cannot determine F. The harmonic oscillator equation gives F→2π at small amplitude; the full simple pendulum supplies its finite-amplitude correction. A model with drag or a finite massive support has additional parameters, so the same dimensional argument does not automatically apply.
The result is useful for comparison: at fixed angular amplitude and g, lengths in the ratio 1:4 give periods in the ratio 1:2. The ratio Tg/ℓ​ should be the same for both in this ideal model. A failure to collapse onto the same value points to measurement error or an omitted parameter. Correct physical dimensions are a necessary consistency check, while the coefficient and the adequacy of the model require more information.

Kepler's laws of planetary motion

Words: 954 Articles: 4
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
Kepler's laws describe three connected features of an elliptic orbit: its shape, how fast it is traversed, and how its size determines its orbital period. Kepler's first law gives an ellipse with the attracting centre at one focus of a conic; Kepler's second law gives equal swept areas in equal times; Kepler's third law relates the squared orbital period to the cubed semi-major axis. Together they turn a drawing of a Kepler orbit into a prediction of where the bodies will be and when they will return. [ref]
Here the mathematical model is an isolated two-body problem in Newtonian gravity, with point masses M,m>0 and a bound, noncolliding elliptic orbit. Let r=rm​−rM​ be the relative displacement, r=∣r∣ the separation, and μ=G(M+m) the gravitational parameter, where G is the gravitational constant. Newton's law of universal gravitation then gives
r¨=−r3μ​r.
(27)
The relative Kepler orbit has semi-major axis a and orbital eccentricity 0≤e<1. Both bodies move around their shared astronomical barycenter, the system's centre of mass. In its rest frame their displacements are rm​=Mr/(M+m) and rM​=−mr/(M+m). Their individual semi-major axes therefore add to a; the relative ellipse's attracting focus of a conic represents zero separation, rather than a body fixed in space.
One example will connect all three laws. After nondimensionalization, choose a=1, e=0.6 and μ=1. The semi-minor axis is b=a1−e2​=0.8, while the periapsis distance and apoapsis distance are
rp​=a(1−e)=0.4,ra​=a(1+e)=1.6.
(28)
Thus a=(0.4+1.6)/2=1 measures the ellipse's size even though the separation changes fourfold. The specific angular momentum will be 0.8, the two endpoint speeds 2 and 0.5, and the orbital period 2π. These are values in the chosen scaled units, not measurements of a particular planet.
Johannes Kepler published Kepler's first law and Kepler's second law in Astronomia Nova in 1609 and Kepler's third law in Harmonices Mundi in 1619. These publication dates are documented by [ref]. Their appeal is that three short statements organize both geometry and timing; Newtonian gravity supplies a common dynamical explanation.

Kepler's first law (r=a(1−e2)/(1+ecosf))

Words: 62
Kepler's laws of planetary motion OurBigBook.com
The bound relative Kepler orbit is an ellipse with the attracting centre at one focus of a conic. In polar coordinates, its separation is the displayed function of true anomaly f, the angle measured from periapsis. For a=1 and e=0.6, it becomes r=0.64/(1+0.6cosf), giving 0.4 at f=0 and 1.6 at f=π. Setting orbital eccentricity to zero gives a circular orbit. This specifies the path; Kepler's second law specifies how it is traversed.

Kepler's third law (T2=4π2a3/[G(M+m)])

Words: 302 Articles: 1
Kepler's laws of planetary motion OurBigBook.com
For an isolated two-body problem in Newtonian gravity, the relative elliptic orbit's orbital period T obeys
T2=G(M+m)4π2a3​=μ4π2a3​.
(29)
Here a is the relative semi-major axis, and M+m is the sum of the two masses. The separation r varies during an elliptic orbit, so replacing a by r works only for a circular orbit, where r=a. Likewise, either body's individual semi-major axis about the centre of mass must first be converted to the relative one. When m is negligible compared with M, the denominator can be approximated by GM.
For fixed gravitational parameter, the orbital period depends on the semi-major axis and is independent of orbital eccentricity. Our a=1, μ=1 example gives T=2π both for e=0.6 and for a circular orbit with e=0. The eccentric body's rapidly changing speed compensates for its different path. A compact way to see the cancellation uses Kepler's second law: divide the ellipse's area πab by its areal velocity h/2. With b=a1−e2​ and specific angular momentum h=μa(1−e2)​, the result is 2πa3/μ​.
Compare two separate Kepler orbits with the same gravitational parameter, a1​=1 and a2​=4:
T1​T2​​=(a1​a2​​)3/2=43/2=8.
(30)
With μ=1, their orbital periods are 2π and 16π; measured in units of T1​, these are 1 and 8. Quadrupling the size therefore takes eight times as long to complete a circuit. This power law makes comparisons possible without first choosing physical units.
The same relation can be inverted to weigh a system: M+m=4π2a3/(GT2). An observed relative semi-major axis and orbital period determine the total mass, while additional information is needed to separate the two masses. This is useful for binary stars, as discussed in NASA, Orbits and Kepler's Laws: measuring masses. Geometry and a clock together become a weighing instrument.

Kepler's second law (dA/dt=h/2)

Words: 308
Kepler's laws of planetary motion OurBigBook.com
The relative displacement of a Kepler orbit sweeps equal areas about the attracting focus of a conic in equal times. A short interval near periapsis covers a wide angle at small separation; the same interval near apoapsis covers a narrow angle at large separation. The swept areas are equal even though the travelled distances are different. In particular, the sectors have curved ellipse boundaries: triangles formed by joining their endpoints only approximate the swept areas for short intervals.
Let h=∣r×r˙∣ be the relative specific angular momentum. The areal velocity is
dtdA​=21​∣r×r˙∣=2h​.
(32)
A central force exerts zero torque about its centre, so conservation of angular momentum makes this rate constant. This explanation also applies to other central forces; the ellipse shape specifically comes from Newtonian gravity.
In the a=1, e=0.6, μ=1 example, specific angular momentum is h=μa(1−e2)​=0.64​=0.8, giving areal velocity 0.4. At periapsis and apoapsis, the velocity is perpendicular to the relative displacement, so h=rv. The endpoint speeds are consequently
vp​=0.40.8​=2,va​=1.60.8​=0.5.
(33)
The fourfold speed difference is consistent with the fourfold separation difference. Away from these endpoints, h/r gives only the transverse component of velocity; the full speed follows from the vis-viva equation.
To actually place equal-time markers, use Kepler's equation. Write mean anomaly as M=nt, with t=0 at periapsis and mean motion n=μ/a3​=1. The different symbol M avoids confusing this angle with the mass M. Solve for eccentric anomaly E in radians, then compute the relative position:
M=E−esinE,x=a(cosE−e),y=bsinE.
(34)
This timing procedure is explained in NASA educational archive, How Orbital Motion is Calculated.
For the first interval 0≤t≤π/6, the final eccentric anomaly is E≈1.041495. For the equal interval π≤t≤7π/6 starting at apoapsis, it ends at E≈3.471065. Both swept areas are ΔA=(h/2)Δt=0.4π/6=π/15≈0.209440, one twelfth of the entire ellipse's area 0.8π. The diagram computes its markers from Kepler's equation, making visible how uniform time steps become uneven spatial steps.

Polarization (waves, E(t)=(Ax​cosωt,Ay​cos(ωt+δ)))

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Wave OurBigBook.com
Polarization of waves describes the direction and time-dependent geometry of a transverse wave's vector during its oscillation at a fixed position. In three spatial dimensions, a transverse wave can have two independent directions of oscillation, both perpendicular to its direction of propagation. For polarization of an electromagnetic wave, the relevant vector is the transverse electric field; for a mechanical transverse wave, it can be the transverse displacement. A purely longitudinal wave has no choice between these transverse directions, and the orientation of a static electric field is not polarization of waves.
Choose transverse axes x,y in a Cartesian coordinate system. A monochromatic wave with a fixed phase difference has the real electric field
E(t)=(Ax​cosωt, Ay​cos(ωt+δ)),Ax​,Ay​≥0,ω>0.
(56)
Here Ax​,Ay​ are wave amplitudes, ω is the angular frequency, and δ is the phase difference of the y oscillation relative to the x oscillation. The vector's tip traces its path during the wave period T=2π/ω. Both plotted coordinates are real electric field components; neither axis represents the imaginary part of a complex amplitude.
For nonzero wave amplitudes, δ=0 or π modulo 2π gives linear polarization: the vector moves back and forth along a fixed line. Equal nonzero wave amplitudes and δ=±π/2 modulo 2π give circular polarization: the tip traces a circle of constant radius. Unequal nonzero wave amplitudes with δ=±π/2 give a noncircular ellipse whose axes coincide with x,y. More generally, nonzero wave amplitudes and sinδ=0 give elliptical polarization, with circular polarization as a special case. If exactly one wave amplitude vanishes, the nonzero wave has linear polarization for every δ; if both vanish, there is no nonzero wave to assign a polarization of waves. [ref].
For example, take ω=2πs−1, so the wave period is T=1s. The choices (Ax​,Ay​,δ)=(2,1,0), (1,1,π/2) and (2,1,π/2), with electric field wave amplitudes in V/m, produce respectively the line segment Ey​=Ex​/2, the circle Ex2​+Ey2​=1 and the ellipse Ex2​/4+Ey2​=1, when coordinates are measured in V/m. At t=T/4, their tips are respectively (0,0), (0,−1) and (0,−1)V/m. The last two share a point without having the same path.
Resolving the electric field into two transverse components makes polarization of waves useful: the same frequency and wave amplitudes can describe different paths when their phase difference changes. An ideal linear polarizer selects the component along its pass axis, letting its orientation probe the direction of linear polarization through Malus's law. A fixed pair of wave amplitudes and a fixed phase difference describe one stable path; unpolarized light requires a statistical description rather than one fixed ellipse.

Elliptical polarization (Ex2​/Ax2​+Ey2​/Ay2​−2Ex​Ey​cosδ/(Ax​Ay​)=sin2δ)

Words: 363
Polarization (waves) OurBigBook.com
For an elliptically polarized wave, the tip of its transverse vector traces an ellipse at a fixed point during each wave period. For polarization of an electromagnetic wave, this is the electric field vector. With the real components in polarization of waves, assume Ax​,Ay​>0 and sinδ=0. Eliminating time gives
Ax2​Ex2​​+Ay2​Ey2​​−Ax​Ay​2Ex​Ey​​cosδ=sin2δ.
(57)
A short derivation uses ϕ=ωt and the cosine addition formula to obtain Ey​/Ay​=(Ex​/Ax​)cosδ−sinϕsinδ; squaring and using the sine and cosine identity sin2ϕ=1−cos2ϕ gives the displayed equation. Outside phase quadrature, the mixed term gives a tilted ellipse; Ax​,Ay​ are component wave amplitudes and need not be its semi-major and semi-minor axes.
In phase quadrature, δ=±π/2, the mixed term vanishes. For (Ax​,Ay​)=(2,1)V/m, the ellipse is Ex2​/4+Ey2​=1, its semi-major and semi-minor axes have lengths 2 and 1V/m, and its electric field magnitude varies between 1 and 2V/m. At ϕ=π/4 with δ=π/2, the electric field is (2​,−1/2​)V/m and has magnitude 5/2​V/m. Equal wave amplitudes instead give circular polarization, a special case of elliptical polarization with constant magnitude. As δ approaches 0 or π, the ellipse collapses to a line segment and gives linear polarization; this limit is degenerate rather than a nondegenerate ellipse.
Changing δ from π/2 to −π/2 reverses traversal of the same ellipse. In the displayed x,y plot, δ=π/2 moves from (Ax​,0) toward negative y as time increases. A label such as right- or left-handed circular polarization additionally requires a stated viewing direction and naming convention: viewing along propagation and viewing against propagation reverse the apparent rotation. [ref].
The ellipse records both the relative wave amplitudes and the phase difference of two transverse oscillations. This separates a change of polarization of waves from a change of overall wave amplitude: multiplying both components by the same positive factor enlarges the ellipse while preserving its shape and orientation.
A rotating ideal linear polarizer can probe this geometry. For the 2:1 ellipse in phase quadrature, orthogonal projection onto a pass axis at angle θ gives Eout​(t)=2cosθcosωt−sinθsinωt, in V/m. Averaging its square over a wave period gives (4cos2θ+sin2θ)/2, while the incoming squared electric field magnitude averages to 5/2. Thus the transmitted fraction of light intensity is (4cos2θ+sin2θ)/5: it is 4/5 at 0∘, 1/2 at 45∘ and 1/5 at 90∘. There is no single incident line of linear polarization to insert into Malus's law; projecting the electric field and averaging its square is the appropriate generalization. This measurement cannot distinguish δ=π/2 from δ=−π/2, because reversing the traversal leaves all these squared averages unchanged.

Malus's law (Iout​=Iin​cos2θ)

Words: 337
Polarization (waves) OurBigBook.com
For incident light with linear polarization, an ideal linear polarizer transmits
Iout​=Iin​cos2θ,
(58)
where I is light intensity and θ is the angle between the incident electric field's line of oscillation and the polarizer's pass axis. The input and output are compared in the same medium. The classical explanation is an orthogonal projection: for a unit vector u along the pass axis,
Eout​=(Ein​⋅u)u.
(59)
The dot product reduces the transmitted wave amplitude by cosθ. For a plane electromagnetic wave in the same medium, light intensity is proportional to squared electric field wave amplitude, giving Malus's law. For example, θ=60∘ transmits one quarter of the incident light intensity, although the transmitted wave amplitude is one half. [ref].
Start with light already in linear polarization along the horizontal 0∘ axis and let its light intensity be I0​. Two ideal absorbing linear polarizers with pass axes 0∘ and 90∘ give I0​cos20∘cos290∘=0. Insert a 45∘ polarizer between them: the first leaves I0​ unchanged, the middle transmits I0​/2 with linear polarization along 45∘, and the last transmits I0​/4 with linear polarization along 90∘. Each angle in Malus's law is relative to the preceding output, so the final step uses 90∘−45∘=45∘:
Iout​=I0​cos20∘cos245∘cos2(90∘−45∘)=4I0​​.
(60)
For these ideal absorbing polarizers, the rejected electric field component transfers energy to the filter. In the three-filter arrangement the middle absorbs the fraction I0​/2, and the last absorbs I0​/4, leaving I0​/4 transmitted. Conservation of energy holds at each step. Inserting the middle polarizer changes the linear polarization arriving at the last one; it does not create light. The effect illustrates why successive orthogonal projections cannot generally be replaced by a single comparison of the first and last axes.
The initially horizontal assumption matters. For unpolarized light of light intensity I0​, the first ideal linear polarizer transmits I0​/2: averaging cos2θ over uniformly distributed incident orientations gives 1/2. The same 0∘,45∘,90∘ sequence then transmits I0​/8. This extra first-stage factor does not apply to the already horizontally polarized input in the figure.

Coherent wave field (m=E[E])
Words: 313 Articles: 3
Wave propagation in a random medium OurBigBook.com
In wave propagation in a random medium, the coherent field is the expectation of the complex wave amplitude, m(r)=E[E(r)]. The remaining field E−m has zero expectation. This is the coherent and diffuse wave fields decomposition. Statistical homogeneity of the medium does not make m spatially constant when the incident field is localized: translation symmetry applies to the response together with its incident data. The coherent component can attenuate while the total ensemble-averaged wave intensity remains substantial.
Gaussian coherent-field propagation in the Markov approximation (m=e−γ(x−x0​)Efree​)
Words: 71
Coherent wave field OurBigBook.com
For the linear weak-index parabolic wave equation, a Markov approximation with integrated covariance B(η)=∫R​C(s,η)ds gives
mx​=2ki​mzz​−γm,γ=2k2μ2B(0)​.
(65)
The drift follows by converting the multiplicative Stratonovich integral ikμE∘dB to an Itô integral for a Brownian field with transverse covariance B. For a Gaussian beam with one transverse coordinate entering the random region at x0​, m(x,z)=e−γ(x−x0​)Efree​(x,z). The coherent field retains transverse beam structure. The white-noise closure needs short longitudinal correlations and the corresponding separation of propagation scales; Gaussian one-point statistics alone are insufficient.
Weak-fluctuation memory equation for the coherent field
Words: 178 Articles: 1
Coherent wave field OurBigBook.com
For a parabolic wave equation with n=1+μW, a zero-mean stationary real field W of unit variance, and L0​=i∂z2​/(2k), finite-correlation perturbation theory gives
mx​​=L0​m+2ikμ2​m−k2μ2∫x0​x​∫R​C(x−s,z−ζ)Gx−s​(z−ζ)m(s,ζ)dζds+O(μ3).​
(66)
Here m is the coherent field, C is the autocorrelation function of a random field and G is the one-coordinate Fresnel propagator. Expand the random solution once using the Duhamel principle, multiply by W and average to obtain the memory term. The local phase term comes from the μ2W2 term in n2. The expansion is for fixed propagation distances with suitable covariance regularity and moment bounds. A Markov approximation is an additional scale assumption that can turn this integral equation into a local attenuation equation.
Quadratic refractive-index shift in the coherent field (∂x​m⊃ikμ2m/2)
Words: 76
Weak-fluctuation memory equation for the coherent field OurBigBook.com
If the physical refractive index is n=1+μW, then n2−1=2μW+μ2W2. In the parabolic wave equation, the last term produces ikμ2E[W2E]/2 in the mean equation. For unit-variance, finite-correlation fluctuations, E[W2E]=m+O(μ) in a weak-fluctuation expansion, giving a coherent phase drift ikμ2m/2 to second order. This term is absent if the model deliberately linearizes n2−1 to 2μW. It is not obtained by squaring ideal Gaussian white noise, whose pointwise square is not the finite-variance random variable W2.

Frequency (ν=1/T)

Words: 31
Wave OurBigBook.com
Frequency is the number of repetitions of a periodic phenomenon per unit time. For a wave of period T, its frequency is ν=1/T, measured in hertz. The angular frequency is ω=2πν.

Doppler effect

Words: 132 Articles: 2
Wave OurBigBook.com
The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency of a wave when source and observer move relative to one another. For light and a small radial recession speed vr​≪c, Δλ/λ≃vr​/c, where λ is wavelength. This is the basis of Doppler spectroscopy.

Relativistic Doppler effect (ν=γν′(1+βcosθ′))

Words: 91 Articles: 1
Doppler effect OurBigBook.com
The Lorentz transformation changes the photon four-momentum and therefore its frequency, producing the displayed formula for a boost along the first axis. Here the primed ray angle is measured in the emitting frame and β=v/c. The angle and frequency transforms must be used together: aberration of light changes the direction, and a photon-number angular fraction need not equal the corresponding radiant-energy fraction.
Kinematic redshift (1+zkin​=(1+v/c)/(1−v/c)​)
Words: 35
Relativistic Doppler effect OurBigBook.com
A kinematic redshift is the relativistic Doppler effect from relative motion of emitter and receiver. With positive radial recession speed v, its small-velocity limit is zkin​=v/c+O(v2/c2). A peculiar velocity gives such a factor in addition to cosmological redshift.

Time evolution

Words: 22
Physics OurBigBook.com
Time evolution describes the change of a physical system's state with time. A closed quantum system has unitary time evolution; dissipative dynamics need not be unitary.
